paragraphs: This paper asks whether modeling several time series together can reveal structure that is difficult to recognize in one series alone. Its starting point is Gaussian process regression, which represents complex changes over time through a covariance kernel. The Automatic Bayesian Covariance Discovery system combines kernels to model a series and produce a natural-language description of its behavior.

The difficulty is that learning a composite kernel from a single series can yield a model whose description is not especially informative or distinctive. The authors propose two relational kernel learning methods that connect multiple time series through shared sources of change. This makes relationships among the series part of the modeling problem, rather than treating each series as an isolated collection of observations.

The reported experiments find more accurate regression models on US stocks, US house price indices, and currency exchange rates. These findings support the value of learning shared structure across related series. The contribution connects the search for descriptive time-series structure with improved regression accuracy on the evaluated real-world datasets.
icml-2016-automatic-construction-of-nonp.tldr: Two relational kernel learning methods improve regression by finding shared structure across multiple time series.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines a collection of rankings into a consensus ranking. Kemeny consensuses are widely regarded as ideal answers to this problem, but computing them is NP-hard. This creates a practical obstacle: even when a candidate ranking is already available, determining how close it is to an ideal consensus can seem to require solving the difficult aggregation problem first.

The paper introduces a practical method for predicting the proximity of Kemeny consensuses to a supplied ranking, using that ranking and the dataset as inputs. Its central move is to assess the relationship to the consensus without first computing the consensus itself. The method rests on a new geometric interpretation of Kemeny aggregation.

A stated strength is that the approach requires no assumptions about either the dataset or the candidate ranking. Its usefulness therefore does not depend on restricting attention to specially structured inputs. The geometric interpretation also offers a potential foundation for further results, although the abstract presents that broader prospect as the authors' expectation.
icml-2016-controlling-the-distance-to-a-.tldr: A geometric approach predicts how close a ranking is to Kemeny consensuses without computing those consensuses.

paragraphs: A time series can change because of influences outside its own history. Weather, events, promotions, and social media trends can all matter for business forecasts, yet the forecasting systems discussed in this paper lack adequate ways to incorporate such information. The authors focus on making multiple external data sources usable within a neural forecasting model.

Their contribution is an attention mechanism that incorporates these sources without the feature engineering needed by other techniques. The approach makes external information part of the forecasting process and also gives the model a greater descriptive ability. This matters because the external factors are useful not only for improving predictions but also for describing what the model takes into account.

The empirical evaluation covers demand for 20 commodities across 107 stores of a large American retailer. The model outperforms the tested neural, linear, kernel, Bayesian regression, and decision-tree baselines. The authors report a 23.9% relative improvement from incorporating external sources, supporting the practical value of this information in the evaluated forecasting setting.
icml-2016-correcting-forecasts-with-mult.tldr: Multifactor neural attention incorporates external data into retail forecasts and delivers a reported 23.9% relative improvement.

paragraphs: The paper develops optimization algorithms for objectives defined on probabilistic models with adjustable parameters. Its focus is the natural gradient, an approach in which the choice of update direction depends on how changes to parameters alter the model's probability distribution. The central design question is how to measure the size of a change between distributions.

Conventional natural gradient methods commonly use the Fisher information matrix. The authors instead derive a new metric tensor from an approximation to energy distance. They obtain their update direction by asking which direction gives the steepest ascent when distributional movement is measured this way. They call the resulting direction the energetic natural gradient.

The distinction is consequential because the measure of distance determines the geometry used by the optimizer. In the authors' formulation, approximated energy distance replaces the role played by Kullback-Leibler divergence in producing the Fisher metric. The proposed class supports both minimization and maximization, and the stated contribution is an alternative natural-gradient construction that uses more information than prior methods.
icml-2016-energetic-natural-gradient-des.tldr: Energetic natural gradients optimize probabilistic models using a metric derived from approximated energy distance.

paragraphs: Disciplined convex programming provides a general framework for expressing convex optimization problems. Existing libraries commonly translate these descriptions into a standard cone form before solving them. This paper develops an alternative route that operates through projections associated with the convex functions used in the problem.

The key operation is an epigraph projection: projecting onto the set of points on or above a convex function's graph. Such operations are closely related to proximal methods. The authors show how these projections can be used to solve any disciplined convex program without the usual conversion to cone form, connecting a general modeling framework to a different collection of computational building blocks.

To make the approach practical, the paper develops a large library of efficient projection operators for common convex functions. Its evaluations show that the resulting algorithm often runs about an order of magnitude faster than existing general-purpose solvers. The finding supports this projection-based route as an effective option across evaluated problems, while retaining the abstract's qualification that the speedups occur often rather than universally.
icml-2016-epigraph-projections-for-fast-.tldr: Fast epigraph projections solve disciplined convex programs without cone conversion and often substantially accelerate optimization.

paragraphs: Segmented regression seeks to recover a function composed of linear pieces from noisy observations. This paper studies the fixed-design version, with recovery accuracy measured by mean-squared error. Earlier approaches with rigorous guarantees use dynamic programming and are efficient in their use of samples, but their running time grows quadratically with the number of observations.

The authors introduce algorithms whose running time is nearly linear in the sample size. Their aim is a better balance between the amount of data required and the computation needed to process it. The algorithms are not minimax optimal, so the contribution explicitly accepts a statistical tradeoff to gain much faster computation on large datasets.

In the experimental comparison, the reported convergence rates differ from those of dynamic programming by factors of two to four, while running times improve by three orders of magnitude. These results illustrate why sample efficiency alone may be an incomplete criterion for choosing a regression method. A moderate loss in convergence rate can accompany a very large practical reduction in computation.
icml-2016-fast-algorithms-for-segmented-.tldr: Nearly linear-time segmented regression algorithms trade some statistical efficiency for large computational gains over dynamic programming.

paragraphs: More complex convolutional networks can improve image recognition while demanding more computation and storage. This paper investigates fixed-point implementations as a way to reduce those demands and potentially support deployment on embedded hardware. The central question is how much numerical precision to allocate to different layers.

The authors design a quantizer and formulate an optimization problem that selects fixed-point bit widths across the network. This makes precision allocation a deliberate optimization decision instead of giving every layer the same bit width. The approach matters because the storage budget can be distributed across layers according to the allocation selected by that optimization.

On CIFAR-10, the optimized allocation reduces model size by more than 20% relative to equal-bit-width settings without losing accuracy in the reported experiments. The authors also find that fine-tuning can raise a fixed-point network's accuracy above that of its original floating-point version. They report a 6.78% error rate, described in the paper as a new state-of-the-art result for fixed-point models on that benchmark.
icml-2016-fixed-point-quantization-of-de.tldr: Optimizing bit widths across convolutional layers reduces model size without accuracy loss in the reported CIFAR-10 experiments.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes convolutional neural networks by building more symmetries into their layers. The proposed Group equivariant Convolutional Neural Networks, or G-CNNs, exploit relationships associated with transformations such as translations, reflections, and rotations. The stated benefit is reduced sample complexity: using symmetry helps the model learn from fewer examples.

The core building block is the G-convolution. It shares weights more extensively than an ordinary convolutional layer, allowing related transformations to use common learned parameters. The authors state that this construction increases expressive capacity without increasing the parameter count. Greater sharing therefore provides a way to strengthen the model's structure without simply making its parameter set larger.

For discrete groups generated by translations, reflections, and rotations, the layers can be implemented with negligible computational overhead. The paper reports state-of-the-art results on CIFAR10 and rotated MNIST. Together, the construction and experiments support explicitly encoding relevant symmetries as a useful architectural choice, with the computational-overhead claim specifically tied to the stated classes of discrete transformations.
icml-2016-group-equivariant-convolutiona.tldr: G-CNNs exploit symmetry through expanded weight sharing, increasing expressive capacity without adding parameters.

paragraphs: Many large machine-learning problems can be expressed as constrained submodular maximization. Distributing these problems across machines seems attractive, but the paper identifies a limitation in existing approaches: the number of instances that must fit in a machine's memory grows with the dataset. Adding machines does not remove that per-machine capacity requirement.

The authors propose a distributed framework that works with fixed capacity. Its goal is to accommodate larger datasets while respecting the physical memory limit of each machine. The framework covers a broad class of algorithms and constraints, and it provides theoretical approximation-factor guarantees for any available capacity. This explicitly connects the quality guarantee to the resources available for the computation.

Experiments on a variety of datasets show performance competitive with a centralized greedy solution. That comparison indicates that distributing the computation under fixed capacity can still produce strong solutions in the evaluated settings. The main contribution is the combination of a practical memory constraint, broad algorithmic applicability, and theoretical control over approximation quality.
icml-2016-horizontally-scalable-submodul.tldr: A distributed submodular maximization framework supports fixed per-machine capacity while providing approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Inference in a directed graphical model works backward from observed variables toward uncertain latent variables. This paper learns an approximate version of that reverse computation so it can be reused. The learned approximation is designed specifically to supply proposal distributions for sequential Monte Carlo, where proposals guide which latent-variable possibilities are explored.

The authors describe how to construct and train a structured neural network representing an inverse factorization of the graphical model. Given particular observed values, the network estimates a conditional distribution over latent variables. Its structure therefore reflects the inference problem, and its output is a distribution that can feed into the sampling procedure.

The recognition network can be trained offline, before inference and independently of a particular dataset. This is the amortization step: a learned inference mechanism can be applied when observations arrive. The paper presents its outputs as automatically learned, high-quality proposals that can accelerate sequential Monte Carlo across diverse settings, linking neural density estimation to an established sampling framework.
icml-2016-inference-networks-for-sequent.tldr: Structured neural inference networks learn reusable proposal distributions to accelerate sequential Monte Carlo in directed graphical models.

paragraphs: The paper studies mixtures of Plackett-Luce models for ranking data. It addresses both whether the underlying mixture can be uniquely identified from rankings and how to learn it efficiently. These questions are connected: an efficient fitting procedure cannot by itself resolve ambiguity when distinct model parameters produce the same observable distribution.

The authors prove that a mixture of k components, for k at least two, is non-identifiable when there are at most 2k−1 alternatives. They show this bound is tight for two components. They also establish a sufficient condition for generic identifiability: k must be no larger than the factorial of floor((m−2)/2), where m is the number of alternatives. Generic identifiability allows exceptional parameter cases.

For mixtures of two components, the paper proposes a generalized method of moments algorithm and proves consistency. Experiments find it significantly faster than the compared EMM algorithm while maintaining competitive statistical efficiency. The work thus combines boundaries on what ranking data can identify with a practical learning method for the two-component case.
icml-2016-learning-mixtures-of-plackett-.tldr: The paper establishes identifiability results for Plackett-Luce mixtures and a consistent, efficient learning algorithm for two components.

paragraphs: Counterfactual inference asks what would have happened under a different choice from the one observed. The paper illustrates this with a patient whose blood sugar might have differed under another medication. It studies such questions using observational data, motivated by the growing availability of records in healthcare, education, employment, and ecology.

The authors propose an algorithmic framework that combines representation learning with ideas from domain adaptation. Representation learning concerns how data are encoded for prediction, while domain adaptation addresses differences between prediction settings. Bringing them together makes the representation of observational data part of the approach to estimating outcomes under alternative choices.

The framework has a theoretical justification and is evaluated against earlier approaches to causal inference from observational data. The authors report that their deep learning algorithm significantly outperforms the previous state of the art in that comparison. The result supports the proposed combination as a promising computational approach to counterfactual questions, with the improvement grounded in the paper's empirical evaluation.
icml-2016-learning-representations-for-c.tldr: A counterfactual inference framework combines representation learning and domain adaptation, with strong reported empirical improvements.

paragraphs: Trajectory optimization methods often alternate between approximating a system's dynamics locally and making a conservative policy update. The paper identifies a potential problem with using a linear approximation of those dynamics: it can bias the policy update and prevent convergence to the optimal policy. The proposed method changes the quantity used to derive the update.

The authors introduce a model-free algorithm that backpropagates a local, time-dependent quadratic Q-function. This local description of action value allows the policy update to be obtained in closed form. The method therefore uses an approximation of the value function to construct its update without relying on the simplifying dynamics assumptions highlighted in the abstract.

A central stated property is exact satisfaction of the KL constraint that controls the policy update. The paper reports improved performance relative to related trajectory optimization algorithms that linearize dynamics. This supports the usefulness of the alternative update construction while keeping the guarantee precise: exact constraint satisfaction is the stated guarantee, rather than a general claim of convergence to a globally optimal policy.
icml-2016-model-free-trajectory-optimiza.tldr: A model-free trajectory optimizer derives closed-form policy updates from local quadratic Q-functions while exactly satisfying a KL constraint.

paragraphs: Planning and reinforcement learning can become computationally difficult when a task contains too many distinct states. State abstraction reduces this burden by grouping situations together while preserving information needed for decisions. Exact abstraction, however, only groups situations that are fully identical in the relevant sense, leaving little room for compression when every situation differs.

The paper investigates approximate abstractions that group nearly identical situations. Allowing a controlled amount of difference creates more opportunities to simplify a task, but it also raises a behavioral question: how much quality can be lost when decisions are based on the compressed representation? The authors provide theoretical guarantees for behaviors derived from four types of approximate abstraction.

Experiments across a variety of environments demonstrate reduced task complexity together with bounded loss of behavioral optimality. The contribution is therefore a way to reason about the tradeoff between a smaller planning problem and the quality of the resulting decisions. Approximation becomes a tool with stated behavioral guarantees, rather than merely a convenience for reducing representation size.
icml-2016-near-optimal-behavior-via-appr.tldr: Approximate state abstractions simplify planning and reinforcement learning with theoretical guarantees on resulting behavior quality.

paragraphs: Saturating activation functions can make neural networks hard to train because their gradients become uninformative or vanish. Dependencies may then be invisible to ordinary stochastic gradient descent, which uses first-order gradients. The paper highlights gating mechanisms as one setting where functions intended to resemble discrete switches can create this difficulty.

The proposed remedy is to inject suitable noise into the problematic portions of the activation function. This can let gradients flow even where the noiseless function would give zero gradients. Larger noise encourages greater exploration, and concentrating it around troublesome regions helps optimization explore the boundary between saturated and better-behaved parts of the function.

The authors also connect gradually reducing the noise to simulated annealing as a way to ease optimization of difficult objectives. Experiments find that noisy replacements help optimization in many settings and achieve competitive or state-of-the-art results across different datasets and tasks. The reported benefits are especially pronounced in difficult training situations, including cases where curriculum learning is needed for good results.
icml-2016-noisy-activation-functions-408.tldr: Adding targeted noise to saturating activations helps gradients and exploration, improving optimization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Partition functions are needed to evaluate and compare probabilistic models, but computing them for complex distributions can be difficult. This paper targets distributions with multiple modes and builds on simulated tempering, a sampling approach that augments the model with an auxiliary inverse-temperature variable.

The proposed estimator uses the probability law of that temperature variable. During sampling, it updates Rao-Blackwellized estimates of the marginal probabilities of inverse temperatures, then expresses the partition-function estimate as a simple quotient of those quantities. This turns information already associated with the tempering process into a mechanism for estimating the model's normalizing quantity.

The authors establish connections with other popular methods and report empirical advantages on large Restricted Boltzmann Machines. In those experiments, their estimates are more accurate than those from Annealed Importance Sampling. They are also accurate enough to track training and validation log-likelihoods during learning at minimal computational cost. That makes the method useful for monitoring a model as it changes, as well as for evaluating a finished model.
icml-2016-partition-functions-from-rao-b.tldr: A tempered-sampling estimator uses inverse-temperature probabilities to estimate partition functions accurately and monitor RBM training.

paragraphs: Extreme classification involves a very large set of possible classes, with only a few labels attached to each example. Methods whose training and prediction costs grow linearly with the class count can become impractical. Existing approaches exploit label relationships through structures such as low-rank matrices or balanced trees, but those assumptions can fail as labels become more diverse.

The paper shows that a margin-maximizing loss combined with an l1 penalty produces highly sparse primal and dual solutions in this setting without sacrificing the predictor's expressive power. The proposed Fully-Corrective Block-Coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm exploits both forms of sparsity, achieving complexity sublinear in the numbers of primal and dual variables. A bi-stochastic search procedure further improves efficiency.

In experiments covering multiclass and multilabel problems, the method achieves significantly higher accuracy than existing extreme-classification approaches while keeping training and prediction times very competitive. The contribution is a route to scalability based on sparsity in the optimization problem, addressing the practical difficulties associated with imposing restrictive structures on label relationships.
icml-2016-pd-sparse-a-primal-and-dual-sp.tldr: PD-Sparse exploits primal and dual sparsity to make extreme classification efficient while preserving expressive power.

paragraphs: PHOG is a generative probabilistic model for program code. It builds on probabilistic context-free grammars, which describe code through grammar productions with associated probabilities. The paper's motivation is that the context useful for predicting a program's structure can extend beyond the parent non-terminal used by those grammars.

The proposed probabilistic higher order grammar allows a production rule to depend on richer context. This expands what the model can capture about programs while retaining the stated learning efficiency of a probabilistic context-free grammar. The important combination is greater contextual modeling power together with a learning procedure that remains comparably efficient.

The authors train PHOG on a large JavaScript corpus and report that it is more precise than existing models while remaining similarly fast. This empirical result supports using richer program context without giving up the speed needed by tools built around probabilistic code models. The paper presents PHOG as a model that can directly benefit such existing programming tools.
icml-2016-phog-probabilistic-model-for-c.tldr: PHOG models richer program context than probabilistic context-free grammars while retaining efficient learning and comparable speed.

paragraphs: Ordered hypothesis testing uses a ranking of hypotheses supplied in advance, from most to least promising. This paper studies how the informativeness of that ordering affects the power of several testing procedures. Its analysis uses an asymptotic framework to distinguish conditions under which an ordering helps from those under which a procedure loses effectiveness.

Accumulation tests, including ForwardStop, can be powerful with a highly informative ordering but become asymptotically powerless under weaker orderings. Selective SeqStep is much less sensitive to ordering quality. In the analyzed regimes, it dominates accumulation tests when the ordering is weak or when non-null hypotheses are sparse or weak.

Motivated by these comparisons, the authors derive Adaptive SeqStep, an improved version of Selective SeqStep. On the GEO-Query dataset, it performs favorably with both good and bad prior orderings. The work shows why choosing an ordered testing procedure should account for the reliability of the ordering and the strength and prevalence of the signals being sought.
icml-2016-power-of-ordered-hypothesis-te.tldr: An analysis of ordering-sensitive testing motivates Adaptive SeqStep, which performs favorably under both good and bad orderings.

paragraphs: Learning a topic model's parameters and inferring the topic proportions of a document are distinct tasks. The paper addresses the latter, where provable algorithms have been harder to develop. It aims to recover the unknown mixture of topics in a document, including when the document contains relatively little text.

The authors exploit a property of topic models to construct simple linear estimators with small variance. Their estimates also identify a point around which the posterior distribution is concentrated. This connects the computationally simple estimate to the model's distribution of plausible topic proportions, providing more justification than a point prediction alone.

The paper also proves lower bounds showing that sufficiently short documents can make hidden-topic recovery information-theoretically impossible. This establishes a real data limitation alongside the positive inference results. Empirically, the algorithm works with realistic topic models, gives good solutions on synthetic data, and takes time comparable to a single Gibbs-sampling iteration. The combined message is efficient, justified inference within the information available in the document.
icml-2016-provable-algorithms-for-infere.tldr: Low-variance linear estimators enable provable topic-proportion inference, alongside lower bounds on what short documents can reveal.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter selection often requires training a model repeatedly and comparing the resulting validation performance. This paper proposes adjusting continuous hyperparameters locally during training instead. It focuses on regularization settings, making their adjustment part of the ongoing learning process rather than relying entirely on separate completed training trials.

The method uses gradients to change hyperparameters so that the model's parameter gradients, and therefore its updates, become more favorable for validation cost. This ties hyperparameter changes to the direction in which training is currently moving the model. Its local character is central: it seeks useful adjustments during optimization rather than claiming a global hyperparameter optimum.

Experiments on MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10 place the learned regularization levels within optimal regions. The tested scheme adds 30% computational overhead regardless of model size, although overall cost depends on how often hyperparameters are updated. The authors report substantially lower computation than similar gradient-based approaches, supporting the method as a practical way to obtain good regularization settings during neural-network training.
icml-2016-scalable-gradient-based-tuning.tldr: Local gradient-based hyperparameter updates find good regularization settings during training with modest reported overhead.

paragraphs: Online prediction in a changing environment calls for a benchmark that can change too. This paper evaluates a predictor against an arbitrarily changing sequence of predictors drawn from a base class. The resulting shifting-regret perspective measures loss relative to an adaptable comparator, reflecting a setting where one fixed predictor may be an inadequate reference.

Earlier results typically handle different base classes separately, including experts and linear predictors on the simplex. The authors introduce an arbitrary mapping within mirror descent to create a common framework. This modification gives them a way to unify and extend results that had been developed for distinct prediction settings.

As a concrete application, the paper proves new shifting-regret bounds for matrix prediction problems. These bounds extend the framework beyond the separately treated examples motivating the work. The contribution is primarily a general analytical and algorithmic construction: it brings changing-comparator guarantees into a shared mirror-descent formulation and demonstrates its reach through new results for matrix-valued prediction.
icml-2016-shifting-regret-mirror-descent.tldr: A modified mirror-descent framework unifies shifting-regret analyses and yields new bounds for matrix prediction.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and slice sampling are two established approaches to Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. This paper connects them through Hamiltonian slice sampling, which performs slice sampling along Hamiltonian trajectories or transformations of those trajectories. The construction combines ideas from the two methods in a single sampling approach.

One theoretical contribution is to clarify a class of model priors that yield slice samplers with closed-form expressions. This identifies structure under which the sampling operation can be expressed directly. The connection is therefore useful both for constructing a sampler and for understanding which prior choices make particular sampling steps tractable.

The method also inherits practical properties from slice sampling: it has fewer tunable hyperparameters than Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and does not require gradient information. The authors demonstrate its out-of-the-box utility on problems ranging from Gaussian process regression to Pitman-Yor mixture models. These examples support its usefulness across different modeling settings, with reduced tuning and gradient requirements as the stated practical advantages.
icml-2016-slice-sampling-on-hamiltonian-.tldr: Hamiltonian slice sampling connects two sampling families while reducing tuning requirements and avoiding the need for gradients.

paragraphs: Computing a graphical model's partition function requires summing weighted contributions over an exponentially large discrete space. This quantity is needed for inference, parameter estimation, and model selection, so its computational difficulty affects several central modeling tasks. The paper proposes an approximation scheme for discrete graphical models whose parameter vectors have bounded norm.

The scheme combines a near-minimax-optimal polynomial approximation of the potential function with a Clenshaw-Curtis-style quadrature. Under the bounded-norm condition, it can estimate the partition function with arbitrarily small error. The authors also randomize the algorithm to divide computation into a high-complexity portion and a low-complexity portion, with the latter potentially executable on small devices.

Experiments find that the randomized algorithm is highly accurate when the parameter norm is small. Otherwise, its performance is comparable to methods whose errors are unbounded. These findings make the role of parameter size concrete: the theoretical approximation framework is accompanied by especially strong empirical accuracy in the small-norm setting, alongside a useful division of computational work.
icml-2016-stochastic-discrete-clenshaw-c.tldr: Polynomial approximation and randomized quadrature estimate partition functions with arbitrarily small error under a bounded-parameter-norm condition.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover relationships among event streams modeled by a multivariate Hawkes process. Its target is the matrix of integrated kernels, which summarizes mutual influences among nodes and encodes causal relationships within the process. The observations can be activity timestamps, such as the times at which users act on a social network.

The authors propose estimating this matrix directly without specifying parametric kernel shapes or estimating the kernels themselves. Their method matches the process's second- and third-order integrated cumulants. This focuses estimation on the aggregate influence relationships, avoiding the need to know or reconstruct the detailed time course of each activity's influence.

A theoretical analysis proves consistency of the estimator. Numerical experiments show robustness to kernel shape, and the paper reports appealing results on MemeTracker and financial order book data. The central contribution is a nonparametric route from timestamp data to the Hawkes process's influence matrix, with both a consistency result and empirical support for reducing dependence on assumptions about kernel shape.
icml-2017-uncovering-causality-from-mult.tldr: A consistent moment-matching method estimates Hawkes influence relationships directly from timestamps without estimating kernel shapes.
